opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the central ones right now. If you look at how we got here, a lot of the progress in post-training came from human preference data: people comparing two answers and saying which one is better. That works remarkably well, but it has a ceiling. Humans get tired, they disagree, and once the model is better than the annotator at, say, a hard math proof or a long piece of code, the signal gets noisy or even misleading.

So I think about it in a few ways. First, you lean on domains where you can verify outcomes. In code you can run tests, in math you can check a proof or a final answer, in games you know who won. Coming from the AlphaGo and AlphaStar world, that's very familiar to me. When you have a clean reward, reinforcement learning can take you well beyond human level, because the system isn't imitating anyone anymore; it's discovering what works.

The harder part is that most of what we care about with language models isn't like Go. There's no win condition for "write a good essay" or "be a helpful research assistant." There, I think the path is models increasingly helping to evaluate models. You train critics, or you use the model itself with lots of thinking time to judge outputs, break a task into checkable pieces, look for errors, and compare alternatives. Evaluation is often easier than generation, so a model can give a useful signal on things it couldn't produce perfectly itself. Humans then move up a level. Instead of labeling every example, they shape the principles, audit the evaluators, and catch where things drift.

You have to be careful, of course. Any reward you optimize hard enough gets exploited. We saw reward hacking constantly in RL, and language models are very creative at finding shortcuts. So part of the research is making reward models robust: ensembles, adversarial testing, grounding in real outcomes wherever possible, and keeping some human oversight in the loop as a check.

Longer term, I'm excited about rewards that come from the world itself. Agents that take actions, run experiments, write software that actually gets used, and get feedback from whether things worked. That's closer to how people learn, and it scales in a way annotation never will. So my short answer is: verification where you can get it, AI-assisted judgment where you can't, and humans steering the whole thing rather than labeling every step.

r001.rationale: The response proposes model-assisted evaluation, but does not say to use those judgments as rewards for reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation is often easier than generation and that a model can provide a useful signal on tasks it could not produce perfectly itself.

r003.rationale: It proposes models evaluating outputs and says humans can shape principles and audit evaluators instead of labeling every example.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions right now, maybe the most important one. If you look at what's worked, what's really driven progress, it's been scale on pretraining, and then increasingly scale on the post-training side, on reinforcement learning. And the bottleneck there is exactly the reward. Where do you get the signal from?

For a while the answer was humans. You collect preferences, you train a reward model, you optimize against it. That got us a long way. But there are obvious limits. Humans are slow, they're expensive, they're inconsistent, and crucially, as the models get better, it becomes very hard for a person to actually tell whether a long mathematical proof is correct, or whether a piece of code is subtly wrong, or whether a thousand-step plan makes sense. So the ceiling you get from human annotation is, roughly speaking, human-level judgment on the thing being judged. And we want to go past that.

So the question is, what else can you use? And I think there are a few directions, and they're not mutually exclusive.

The first one, which is the one that's clearly working today, is verifiable domains. Math, code, anything where you can run it, check it, execute it. The nice thing there is the reward is essentially free and essentially perfect. You don't need a human to tell you the unit tests passed. And we've seen, I think, that this transfers more than people expected. Training on hard reasoning problems with clean reward makes the model better at things that aren't math and code. So one strategy is just to keep expanding the set of things that are verifiable, build more environments, more simulators, more ways to ground the model in something that pushes back.

The second direction is using the models themselves as judges. And I know people are skeptical, because there's this circularity, right, the model grading the model. But I'd point out that verification is often easier than generation. It's easier to check a proof than to come up with it. It's easier to spot a bug than to write the program. So you can have an asymmetry where the judge, even if it's the same base model, is operating on a simpler problem, and that gap is something you can exploit. The research question is how to keep the judge honest, because the policy will find any weakness in it. That's the whole game with RL. It will exploit you.

And then the third thing, which is where I think it gets more interesting, is making the reward itself something that gets learned and improved in the loop, rather than fixed up front. You can imagine a system where the model proposes problems, attempts them, checks them, and the checking process is itself being refined. This is closer to the AlphaGo story, where self-play gave you an unbounded signal because the environment was the game. The difficulty with language is that the world isn't a board game with a clear win condition. So part of the work is constructing those conditions, finding tasks that have the structure of a game even if they look like open-ended problems.

I'd also say we shouldn't throw out humans entirely. I think the role changes. Instead of labeling every example, humans end up specifying what we care about at a higher level, catching the failure modes, auditing the judges. It's more like supervision of the supervisor.

But overall, if you ask me where the next few years go, I think the answer is that the reward signal increasingly comes from the environment and from the models themselves, with humans setting the direction rather than grading the homework. And whoever figures out how to do that robustly, without the model gaming the reward, probably ends up with the best models.

r001.rationale: The response identifies models as judges and describes reward increasingly coming from models themselves in the reinforcement-learning context.

r002.rationale: It says verification is often easier than generation and gives proof-checking and bug-spotting as examples, including when the judge uses the same base model.

r003.rationale: It contrasts model judging with the limits of human annotation and says humans would no longer label every example, reducing the need for task-specific labels.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that human annotation is one source of signal, but it’s not the only one. If you look at something like AlphaGo, we didn’t need a human to tell us whether every move was good. We had the rules of the game, and we knew who won. That gives you a signal you can use to discover things that even the best human players didn’t know.

For language models, there are domains where you can get a similar signal. If you write a program, you can execute it and check whether it passes tests. If you’re solving a mathematical problem, sometimes you can verify the answer or the proof. The interesting thing is that verifying a solution can be much easier than generating it. So the system can potentially produce something beyond what a human annotator could have demonstrated, while still getting useful feedback.

Of course, for something like, ‘Was this conversation helpful?’ there isn’t a simple win condition. There, I think you’ll have a combination of human feedback, learned reward models, and feedback from what actually happens when you use the answer. And you have to be careful: optimizing a reward model can make you very good at exploiting its mistakes. So improving the reward and checking that it still measures what we care about have to happen alongside improving the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes execution and verification as feedback sources, but does not say language models use their own judgments as reinforcement-learning rewards.

r002.rationale: It says verification can be easier than generating a solution, but does not clearly state that language models can evaluate their own outputs more accurately than they generate them.

r003.rationale: It mentions learned reward models alongside human feedback, but does not say that using language models as reward models would reduce task-specific annotations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human annotation is a starting point, but it’s not necessarily the ceiling. In games, for example, you don’t need a human to tell you whether every move was good. You have an outcome, and you can learn strategies that go beyond what the people who designed the game could have demonstrated.

For language models, the question is where we can get similarly reliable feedback. Code is a nice example: you can run it, test it, and see whether it actually solves the problem. In mathematics, sometimes you can verify a proof. Those signals let you improve without asking a person to judge every answer.

The harder part is extending that to things where success is less clear. You can use models to critique other models, or help humans evaluate answers they couldn’t easily evaluate on their own. But then you have to be careful that you’re improving the underlying capability rather than just getting better at satisfying the judge. So I think progress comes from combining human judgment with feedback from the world, and gradually making that feedback more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response mentions models critiquing other models, but does not propose reinforcement learning that uses a model’s own judgments as rewards.

r002.rationale: It does not say that checking correctness can be easier than producing a solution or that models may judge their outputs more accurately than they generate them.

r003.rationale: It describes code and proof verification as feedback signals, but does not suggest using language models as reward models to reduce task-specific annotations.
